title: Integrals that run to infinity
objectives: Evaluate improper integrals and decide when they converge.
Show that $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$
Value a perpetual cash stream as $\int_0^\infty e^{-rt}\,dt$

screens.prose: The curve $\frac{1}{x^2}$ falls towards 0 but never reaches it. The shaded strip runs from $x = 1$ to $x = b$. Slide $b$ far out and watch the area.
screens.question: As $b$ grows without limit, what happens to the area?

options.text: It grows without limit, because the strip never ends
options.why: The strip is endless, but it thins fast. The caption creeps up and stalls below 1.
At $b = 1000$ the caption shows 0.9990. It gets as close to 1 as we like, but never reaches it.

hints.text: The area gains less and less as $b$ grows.

feedback.correct: The area closes in on 1 and never passes it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the area for larger and larger $b$.

explain.text: The caption read 0.9 at $b = 10$, 0.99 at 100 and 0.999 at 1000. An endless strip can have a finite area when it thins fast enough. Here the area closes in on 1.

screens.prose: The caption computed $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$. Its limit as $b \to \infty$ is written $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$, an **improper integral**. When the limit is finite, the integral **converges**.
screens.question: Find $\displaystyle\int_1^b \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ in terms of $b$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the antiderivative $-\frac{1}{x}$ and evaluate from 1 to $b$.

byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. It is $F(b) - F(1)$, and the area must be positive.
byKey.power-up: You raised the power to $-3$. Integrating $x^{-2}$ raises it by one, to $x^{-1}$.
byKey.upper-only: You evaluated at $b$ only. At $x = 1$, $-\frac{1}{x} = -1$, so subtract it.

explain.text: $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = 1 - \frac{1}{b}$, and $\frac{1}{b} \to 0$ as $b \to \infty$. So $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = 1$: the improper integral converges to 1. Always compute $\int_1^b$ first, then let $b$ grow.

screens.prose: Now the steeper curve $\frac{1}{x^3}$, drawn under the dashed $\frac{1}{x^2}$. It thins out even faster.
screens.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^3}\,dx$.

hints.text: $-\frac{1}{2b^2} + \frac{1}{2}$, and the first term tends to 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate from 1 to $b$ first, then let $b \to \infty$.

byKey.one-over-p: You divided by 3. Integrating $x^{-3}$ gives $\frac{x^{-2}}{-2}$: divide by the new power, $-2$.
byKey.same: That is the area under $\frac{1}{x^2}$. The steeper curve encloses less.
byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. The curve is above the axis, so the area is positive.

explain.text: $\int_1^b x^{-3}\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2b^2}$, which tends to $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The steeper curve sits below $\frac{1}{x^2}$, so its area is smaller than 1. Faster thinning means less area.

screens.prose: Now a slower curve, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2}$. It also falls towards 0. Here $\int_1^b x^{-1/2}\,dx = 2\sqrt{b} - 2$.
screens.question: What does $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ do?

options.why: You dropped $2\sqrt{b}$ as if it vanished. It grows without limit as $b$ grows.
The curve is above the axis, so no area under it is negative. And $2\sqrt{b}$ does not vanish.

hints.text: $2\sqrt{b} - 2$ has no finite limit, so the integral diverges.

feedback.correct: $2\sqrt{b} - 2$ grows without limit, so the integral diverges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $2\sqrt{b} - 2$ does as $b$ grows.

explain.text: At $b = 100$ the area is 18; at $b = 10\,000$ it is 198. It never settles, so the integral **diverges**. The curve falls to 0, but too slowly.

screens.prose: The middle case is $\frac{1}{x}$, which also falls to 0 as $x$ grows. Slide $b$ and watch the area from 1 to $b$.
screens.question: Does $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ converge?

options.why: Falling to 0 is not enough. The area is $\ln b$, which grows without limit.
That is $\ln 1000$, the area up to $b = 1000$. At $b = 10^6$ it is 13.8, and it keeps growing.

options.text: No: the area is $\ln b$, which grows without limit

hints.text: An antiderivative of $\frac{1}{x}$ is $\ln x$. What is $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx$?
$\ln b$ grows slowly but without limit: $\ln 10^6 \approx 13.8$, $\ln 10^{12} \approx 27.6$.

feedback.correct: $\ln b$ has no finite limit, so the integral diverges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ and ask what it does as $b$ grows.

byKey.zero: You assumed a curve that falls to 0 has finite area. $\frac{1}{x}$ falls to 0, yet $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln b$ grows without limit.
byKey.value: You read the area at one value of $b$. Convergence asks about every $b$, and $\ln b$ keeps growing.

explain.text: $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln b$, and $\ln b \to \infty$, however slowly. So a function can fall to 0 and still have infinite area. $\frac{1}{x}$ sits exactly on the boundary between converging and diverging.

screens.prose: For $p \neq 1$, $$\int_1^b x^{-p}\,dx = \frac{b^{1-p} - 1}{1 - p}.$$ The term $b^{1-p}$ decides everything. Slide $p$ and $b$ to test it.

derive.caption: $p$ = {{p}}: area from 1 to {{b}} is {{abs(p - 1) < 0.001 ? fixed(ln(b), 3) : fixed((pow(b, 1 - p) - 1) / (1 - p), 3)}}

screens.question: Which values of $p$ give a finite $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$?

options.why: At $p = 1$ the area is $\ln b$, which grows without limit. The boundary case diverges.
Every $p > 0$ makes the curve fall to 0. At $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ the area still grows like $2\sqrt{b}$.

hints.text: When does $b^{1-p}$ shrink to 0 as $b$ grows?
It shrinks when the power $1 - p$ is negative.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $p = 1$ and $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ with the sliders.

byKey.ge: You included $p = 1$. That case is $\ln b$, which diverges.

explain.text: For $p > 1$ the power $1 - p$ is negative, so $b^{1-p} \to 0$. For $p < 1$ it grows, and $p = 1$ gives $\ln b$. So $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$.

screens.prose: Finish the line for $p > 1$, where $b^{1-p} \to 0$: $$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \frac{b^{1-p} - 1}{1 - p} = \frac{0 - 1}{1 - p} = \;?$$
screens.question: Write the value as a fraction in $p$ with a positive bottom.

widget.label: The value of the integral, in p

hints.text: Multiply the top and bottom by $-1$.

feedback.correct: $\frac{-1}{1 - p} = \frac{1}{p - 1}$, which is 1 at $p = 2$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at $p = 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip the sign of the top and the bottom of $\frac{-1}{1 - p}$.

byKey.sign: That is negative for $p > 1$, but the area is positive. The top's minus sign moves to the bottom.
byKey.one-over-p: You divided by $p$. The antiderivative of $x^{-p}$ divides by the new power, $1 - p$.

explain.text: Dividing $-1$ by $1 - p$ gives $\frac{1}{p - 1}$. It matches the screens before: 1 at $p = 2$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at $p = 3$. As $p$ falls towards 1 the value blows up, the edge of divergence.

screens.prose: A perpetuity pays £1 a year forever, arriving continuously. At a 4% continuous discount rate, money at time $t$ is worth $e^{-0.04t}$ today. Its value is $\int_0^\infty e^{-0.04t}\,dt$.

derive.caption: Value of the first {{T}} years: {{money((1 - exp(-0.04 * T)) / 0.04)}}

screens.question: What is the perpetuity worth today?

hints.text: Over $[0, b]$ the value is $\frac{1 - e^{-0.04b}}{0.04}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate from 0 to $b$, then let $b \to \infty$.

byKey.times-rate: You multiplied 0.04 by 100. The integral divides by the rate: $\tfrac{1}{0.04}$.
byKey.rate: That is the rate itself. The value is its reciprocal, $\tfrac{1}{0.04}$.
byKey.sign: You lost a sign. $\left[-\tfrac{e^{-0.04t}}{0.04}\right]_0^b = \tfrac{1}{0.04} - \tfrac{e^{-0.04b}}{0.04}$, which is positive.

explain.text: Over $[0, b]$ the value is $\frac{1 - e^{-0.04b}}{0.04}$, and $e^{-0.04b} \to 0$. So the perpetuity is worth $\frac{1}{0.04} = \text{£}25.00$. In general $\int_0^\infty e^{-rt}\,dt = \frac{1}{r}$.

screens.prose: Now the payment starts at £1 a year and grows at 2% a year continuously. Discounting at 4%, its value is $$\int_0^\infty e^{0.02t}\,e^{-0.04t}\,dt.$$
screens.question: What is the growing perpetuity worth today?

hints.text: This is the last screen's integral with rate $r = 0.02$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Combine the two exponentials first.

byKey.no-growth: That ignores the growth. The payments rise, so the stream is worth more than the flat £25.00.
byKey.added: You added the rates: $\tfrac{1}{0.06}$. Growth works against discounting, so subtract: $0.04 - 0.02$.

explain.text: The integrand is $e^{-0.02t}$, so the value is $\frac{1}{0.04 - 0.02} = \text{£}50.00$. This is the continuous Gordon growth formula, $\frac{1}{r - g}$. If growth reached 4% the integrand would not fall at all, and the integral would diverge.

ideas: An integral to infinity is the limit of $\int_a^b$ as $b \to \infty$. It converges when that limit is finite.
$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$, and then equals $\frac{1}{p - 1}$.
A perpetual £1 a year at rate $r$ is worth $\int_0^\infty e^{-rt}\,dt = \frac{1}{r}$: £25.00 at 4%.
summary.trap: A curve that falls to 0 can still have infinite area: $\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln b$ grows without limit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the 3 outside, then use $\tfrac{1}{p - 1}$ with $p = 4$.

byKey.one-over-p: You used $\tfrac{1}{p}$. Integrating $x^{-4}$ divides by $-3$, so the factor is $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
byKey.no-three: That is $\int_1^\infty x^{-4}\,dx$. Multiply by the 3 on top.

explain.text: $\int_1^\infty x^{-4}\,dx = \tfrac{1}{3}$, since $p = 4 > 1$. Times 3, the integral is 1.

quiz.prose: Four improper integrals, each starting at $x = 1$.
quiz.question: Which one converges?

options.why: Here $p = 0.99 < 1$, so $b^{1-p} = b^{0.01}$ grows without limit, slowly.
This is $\ln b$, which grows without limit. The boundary case diverges.
Here $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and the area grows like $2\sqrt{b}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the one with $p > 1$.

explain.text: Only $p = 1.01$ exceeds 1, so only that integral converges, to $\frac{1}{1.01 - 1} = 100$. Close to the boundary, convergence can be slow and the value large.

quiz.prose: A stream pays £5 a year forever, continuously, discounted at 10% a year continuously.
quiz.question: What is it worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\int_0^\infty e^{-rt}\,dt = \tfrac{1}{r}$ and multiply by 5.

byKey.times: You multiplied 5 by 0.1. The integral divides by the rate.
byKey.no-discount-factor: That is one year's payment. The stream pays forever.

explain.text: $\int_0^\infty 5e^{-0.1t}\,dt = 5 \times \frac{1}{0.1} = \text{£}50.00$. A higher discount rate would make it worth less.

quiz.question: What can you conclude about $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx$?

options.why: $\frac{1}{x}$ falls to 0, yet its integral is $\ln b$, which diverges.
$\frac{1}{x^2}$ falls to 0, and its integral converges to 1.

options.text: Nothing yet: it depends on how fast $f$ falls

feedback.correct: Falling to 0 allows both outcomes: $\frac{1}{x^2}$ converges and $\frac{1}{x}$ diverges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test your answer on $\frac{1}{x}$ and on $\frac{1}{x^2}$.

explain.text: $\frac{1}{x^2}$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ both fall to 0. The first has finite area, the second does not. So $f \to 0$ alone decides nothing; the speed of the fall does.
